lessons.title: This week's storylines
lessons.objective: Explain what is being discussed in hockey right now.

payload.prompt: When fans talk about hockey 'this week', what are they most likely discussing?

options.text: Streaks, injuries to key players, trades or big trades rumors.
The history of the sport and past championships.
How to improve your skating technique.

explanation.correct: Right. Current events like streaks, injuries, trades and controversies are what fans talk about this week.
explanation.incorrect: This week is always about what is happening right now: who is hot, who is hurt, what deal just went down.
explanation.sayThisLine: So what is the big story in hockey this week?

payload.prompt: A player with 6 goals in the last five games is in a slump.

scene.alt: A player has scored 6 goals recently.

explanation.correct: False. Six goals in five games is a hot streak, not a slump. That is exciting news and a story for the week.
explanation.incorrect: That pace is a hot streak. A slump is when a scorer goes cold.

statement.speaker: Riley
statement.text: Our top line is on fire right now. Three games, 12 points between them.

payload.question: What is she telling you?

options.text: Her team's best players have been scoring a lot recently.
options.explanation: Correct. 'On fire' means playing great, and 12 points in three games is hot scoring.

options.text: The team is literally in danger.
options.explanation: This is hockey talk, not a literal fire. She means the players are scoring well.

options.text: The top line usually scores this much.
options.explanation: 'On fire' means playing exceptionally well, better than usual.

payload.translation: Her team's best line has been scoring at a great pace this week.

followUps.line: Are they ahead in the playoff race?
followUps.why: Connects hot play to what it means for the season.

followUps.line: Who is leading the team in scoring?
followUps.why: Asks her to name the player, showing you are following the storylines.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Streaks, hot scoring and slumps are the weekly topics fans care about.

payload.prompt: Complete the fan conversation about injuries.

options: This is big for the playoff race
gaps.correct: This is big for the playoff race

explanation.correct: Right. A key player out mid-season is a top-of-the-week story; it changes the team's odds.
explanation.incorrect: An injury to a star is a major talking point; it affects playoff hopes and depth.

lessons.title: Reading the standings today
lessons.objective: Interpret the live standings table and what {{team}}'s position means.

payload.prompt: In the NHL, a team wins 3-2 in regulation. How many standing points do they get?

options.text: 1 point (for the score).
2 points (for the win).
3 points (for the score).

explanation.correct: Correct. A regulation win is 2 points. A win in overtime or a shootout is 2 points for the winner, 1 for the loser.
explanation.incorrect: The NHL points system: 2 for a win (regulation or overtime/shootout), 0 for a loss, 1 for an overtime/shootout loss (the loser point).
explanation.sayThisLine: In the standings, look at wins and points, not just the score.

payload.prompt: {{team}} is 3 points out of a wild-card spot. How many games would it take to make up that gap if they won every game?

explanation.correct: Exactly 2 games. Two wins = 4 points, which beats a 3-point gap. Math: 2 wins x 2 points = 4 points.
explanation.incorrect: Each win is worth 2 points. To gain 3 points, you need at least 2 wins (4 points): 4 - 3 = 1 point clear.

payload.prompt: Two teams are tied on points in the standings. What is the first tiebreaker in the NHL?

options.text: Regulation wins (RW).
Head-to-head record.
Alphabetical order.

explanation.correct: Yes. Regulation wins is the first tiebreaker. RW ignores overtime losses, so it rewards winning in 60 minutes.
explanation.incorrect: The first tiebreaker is regulation wins (RW), then regulation and overtime wins (ROW). Head-to-head is down the list.

statement.speaker: Sarah
statement.text: We are 5 points out with a game in hand. We can still make the wild card.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: Her team is 5 points behind a wild-card spot but has played fewer games.
options.explanation: Correct. 'Game in hand' means one fewer game played, so they can close the gap.

options.text: Her team has 5 extra games left.
options.explanation: 'Game in hand' means one fewer game played, not five extra games.

options.text: The wild card is decided by one game.
options.explanation: A game in hand is an advantage in the standings, not a decision rule.

payload.translation: They are 5 points behind the last playoff spot but have fewer games played, so catching up is possible.

followUps.line: How many games does your team have left?
followUps.why: Moves to the concrete math of how much time they have.

followUps.line: Who is the team holding that wild-card spot?
followUps.why: Shows you are tracking the race.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: A game in hand is a real advantage; it is a talking point in tight races.

lessons.title: The playoff race
lessons.objective: Explain who is in, out and on the bubble in the {{league}} playoff push.

payload.prompt: In the NHL, how many wild-card teams from each conference make the playoffs?

options.text: 1 wild card per conference.
2 wild cards per conference.
3 wild cards per conference.

explanation.correct: Right. Two wild cards from each conference. The three division winners qualify automatically, plus two wild cards from the remaining teams.
explanation.incorrect: The format is three division winners and two wild cards per conference, for eight teams total per conference (16 in the playoffs).
explanation.sayThisLine: The wild card is the last playoff spot; it goes to the next-best team outside the divisions.

payload.prompt: Your team is 2 points out with 20 games left. What happens next is up to them.

situation.narrative: {{team}} is on the playoff bubble with plenty of season left.

facts.label: Injuries
facts.value: Top center out two more weeks

options.label: They need to panic and make a trade now.
options.consequence: Overreacting this early often backfires. The team has time to make up ground.

options.label: Give it another 10 games; then reassess.
options.consequence: You learn more about whether the team can close the gap without a trade.
considerations: Still time to trade at the deadline
The injury should heal by then

options.label: Sell the veterans and plan for next year.
options.consequence: The team is still in it; sellers give up too early and waste what they have.

payload.expertNote: Teams on the bubble make their biggest moves near the trade deadline, not mid-season panic buys.

statement.speaker: Alex
statement.text: We're on the bubble. One bad week and we could fall out.

payload.question: What does he mean?

options.text: The team is close to the last playoff spot and a losing streak could end their chances.
options.explanation: Correct. 'On the bubble' means skating right at the playoff line, vulnerable to a slide.

options.text: The team is guaranteed to miss the playoffs.
options.explanation: 'On the bubble' means they are still in the race, just tightly.

options.text: The team has actually made the playoffs already.
options.explanation: On the bubble is the opposite; they are not yet safe.

payload.translation: The team is sitting right at the playoff line. They are in, but a slide could knock them out.

followUps.line: How many points do they have in their last 10?
followUps.why: Asks for the trend, which affects their chances.

followUps.line: Who's team ahead of them in the race?
followUps.why: Shows you are tracking the pack.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: The bubble is tense; teams fight hard to stay in the race.

payload.prompt: Match the playoff race term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: A team is skating right at the playoff line, in the race but vulnerable to dropping out.
One of two playoff spots per conference that go to non-division-winners.
A team is too far behind to realistically make the playoffs.

explanation.summary: The playoff race has clear language: bubble, wild card and out.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ask her where her team sits in the race and use these terms.

lessons.title: Watching a live game
lessons.objective: Follow {{team}}'s game in progress and understand what matters.

payload.prompt: You're watching and it's 2-2 late in the third. Your team has more shots. What matters now?

options.text: Time on the clock and the flow of play in the final minutes.
How many shots each team has taken.
The total cost of the teams' rosters.

explanation.correct: Yes. In tight late games, every minute and shift matters. Watch for momentum and who controls the puck in the final stretch.
explanation.incorrect: Late in a tie game, you watch the clock, the period, and who has the puck. Shot totals tell a story over 60 minutes, but the moment matters most now.

payload.prompt: Your team is down 1-0 with three minutes left. They get a power play. What happens first?

options.text: The goalie comes out for an extra skater.
The team sets up the five-on-four with a formation.
The puck drops for a faceoff.

explanation.correct: Right. The faceoff starts the power play. Then the team sets up into a formation (1-3-1, umbrella, overload) to work the puck.
explanation.incorrect: A power play starts with a faceoff, then the team shapes up into a formation to create scoring chances.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: They scored, but we still have all the momentum.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: Her team is outplaying the other team even though they are behind in the score.
options.explanation: Correct. Momentum is about flow and control, not the scoreboard. She thinks her team will score next.

options.text: The other team's goal was meaningless.
options.explanation: A goal counts; she just means her team is playing better.

options.text: Momentum can be measured mathematically.
options.explanation: Momentum is feel and flow, not a statistic.

payload.translation: Her team is playing well and creating chances; one goal down does not mean they will lose.

followUps.why: Time left determines how much momentum matters.

followUps.line: Are they getting good scoring chances?
followUps.why: Helps measure whether the momentum is real.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Momentum is real in games; it is about who is controlling play and who looks tired.

payload.prompt: It is 4-3 with 90 seconds left and {{team}} is down. They pull the goalie for an extra skater.

scene.alt: The goalie is off the ice and an extra attacker replaces him.

explanation.correct: Right. With under two minutes left and down one, pulling the goalie is a reasonable gamble for the tie or the go-ahead.
explanation.incorrect: Late in a tie game down one, pulling the goalie is a standard move. It is an aggressive bet on scoring versus giving up an empty netter.

lessons.title: The hockey calendar
lessons.objective: Explain what happens each month and where the season is now.

payload.prompt: When does the NHL regular season start each year?

options.text: Early September.
Late September or early October.
November.

explanation.correct: Right. The NHL preseason starts in September; the regular season kicks off in late September or early October.
explanation.incorrect: Preseason is September; the regular season starts late September or early October and runs through April.

payload.prompt: Put these hockey events in order as they happen during a season.

explanation.correct: Right. Preseason, then regular season with the deadline mid-season, then playoffs and the draft.
explanation.incorrect: The order is preseason, regular season (with the deadline in March), playoffs, and draft.
explanation.sayThisLine: The trade deadline is always a big moment; it is when teams show whether they are buying or selling.

payload.prompt: Why is the trade deadline important?

options.text: It is when teams decide whether to buy a renter or sell for picks.
It marks the end of the regular season.
It is when the draft lottery happens.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Contenders buy, sellers trade away veterans for draft picks. The deadline is the biggest trading day.
explanation.incorrect: The deadline is a strategic moment: teams race to add depth (rentals) or start rebuilding (selling veterans for picks).

payload.prompt: Complete the statement about the NHL Draft.

explanation.correct: Right. The draft is where teams pick 18-year-old prospects after the Cup Final.
explanation.incorrect: Teams hold the draft after the season to add young talent to their system.

lessons.title: Trade deadline talk
lessons.objective: Explain why a trade at the deadline matters and the {{team}} strategy.

statement.speaker: Coach
statement.text: We got a rental: a winger on an expiring deal who leaves in July.

payload.question: What is he saying?

options.text: A player with a contract that ends this summer, bought for a short playoff run.
options.explanation: Correct. A rental is a temporary help: the team gets a boost now, but the player is a free agent soon.

options.text: The team is renting an arena.
options.explanation: In trade talk, a rental is a player on an expiring contract.

options.text: The player will stay forever.
options.explanation: A rental leaves in the summer; the deal is short-term help.

payload.translation: A rental is a player on a deal ending this year. The team pays picks for a playoff boost; he moves on in the summer.

followUps.line: What does the team give up for a rental?
followUps.why: Moves to the cost of the trade.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Rentals are a deadline staple; every contender uses them to add depth before the playoffs.

payload.prompt: Trade deadline: your favorite team is 5 points out with 15 games left.

situation.narrative: The team is just inside the playoff race and must choose.

facts.label: Stars
facts.value: Two key players on expiring deals

options.label: Buy a rental to make one last push.
options.consequence: You use the cap space to add depth and gamble on the team finding form.

options.label: Hold still and see if the team can catch up on its own.
options.consequence: You conserve assets but risk falling further back.

options.label: Trade the veterans for picks and plan for next year.
options.consequence: You tear down too early when the team is still in it.

payload.prompt: A player has a cap hit of $6 million but earns $8 million in salary. Why do teams care about the cap hit?

options.text: The cap hit is what counts against the salary cap limit.
The cap hit is the player's actual paycheck.
The cap hit is what the team wants to pay.

explanation.correct: Right. The salary cap counts the cap hit, not the actual salary. That difference can be a tool for trades and contracts.
explanation.incorrect: Cap hit is the average annual value used by the league's salary cap accounting. A player's salary might be different in different years.

payload.prompt: A rental is always the better choice than a long-term player for the deadline.

scene.alt: Two players: one on a rental deal, one under contract long-term.

explanation.correct: False. It depends on the team's situation. A contender wants a rental for a playoff run. A team rebuilding wants to keep young players.
explanation.incorrect: Rentals are good for contenders in a playoff push. They are not always the right fit for every team's strategy.

lessons.title: Playoff mode
lessons.objective: Explain playoff intensity and what a series win means for {{team}}.

statement.speaker: Fan
statement.text: It's Game 7 tomorrow. Winner take all.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: The final game of a best-of-seven series decides who moves on.
options.explanation: Correct. Game 7 is the decider; whoever wins advances.

options.text: They are playing seven games no matter what.
options.explanation: If a team wins 4 games first, the series ends early. Game 7 only happens if it goes to 3-3.

options.text: This is a regular-season game.
options.explanation: Game 7 is playoff only; it is the most intense matchup.

payload.translation: It is the final, deciding game. The winner advances; the loser is eliminated.

followUps.why: Home ice is a big playoff edge.

followUps.line: How are they up in the series?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Game 7 is playoff folklore; every fan remembers them.

payload.prompt: In a best-of-seven playoff series, how many wins does a team need to advance?

options.text: Three wins.
Four wins.
Five wins.

explanation.correct: Right. Four wins in a best-of-seven. First to four wins advances; the series ends as soon as one team reaches four.
explanation.incorrect: First to four. If one team wins 4 before 7 games are played, the series is over.

payload.prompt: Why do teams value home ice advantage in the playoffs?

options.text: The home crowd provides energy and the team plays one more home game if the series goes seven.
The home team's goalie is always better.
The home team gets to choose the goal horn.

explanation.correct: Yes. Home ice means more home games, crowd energy and the last game is at home if needed. It is a real edge in playoffs.
explanation.incorrect: Home ice is valuable: you host more games and the final game at home (if it reaches Game 7) is a huge advantage.
